newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Hoogovens seen approaching fair value.
newsitem.headline: Hoogovens seen approaching fair value.

text.p: Shares of Dutch steel group Hoogovens have risen sharply in recent weeks, leading some analysts to conclude they now trade at or near their fair value.
Up to the end of October Hoogovens shares had lagged the AEX Dutch share market index, but a rise of over 18 percent since then has turned them into an outperformer.
"I'm maintaining a 'hold' on Hoogovens because I think the rally is probably over," said Terence Sinclair of Salomon Bros.
Sinclair said Hoogovens' cash flow of 12 percent of sales in 1992-95 was one of the highest in the sector, compared with 4.3 percent for Arbed and 6.6 percent for Thyssen.
"But that's already in the Hoogovens price... I think the shares are fairly valued," he said.
Sinclair said Hoogovens' did not look expensive relative to its peers, but added that there was little to distinguish it.
He estimates that Hoogovens shares trade around 7.2 times 1997 earnings compared with 6.6 times for British Steel.

On the basis of enterprise value (market capitalisation plus debt) divided by 1997 EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation), Hoogovens even looked a little cheaper at 2.9 than Usinor Sacilor on 3.5, he said.
Sinclair said his favourite steel shares were Acerinox, a Spanish stainless steel producer, and Usinor, which he said both looked cheap on the basis of 1998 EBITDA multiples.
Quirijn Mulder of ING Barings said recent gains had pushed Hoogovens' share price towards a fairer value, better reflecting the firm's potential for a strong rebound in earnings next year.
In November, with the shares at 60 guilders, he recommended them as a buy, saying they were undervalued on several measures relative to British Steel, Usinor Sacilor and Arbed.
The shares have since travelled much of the way to the target price of 75 guilders which ING Barings had set for them.
Mulder said efficiency gains and enhanced profitability would pave the way for a jump in Hoogovens' earnings per share to 11.41 guilders in 1997 and 17.77 in 1998 from 8.40 in 1996.
But he would like to see the company sell off its aluminium division, arguing that its returns are lower than its cost of capital and that this was destroying economic value added (EVA).
"We believe that a divestment of Hoogovens Aluminium would be positive for the group as a whole," he said.

Peter Dupont of UBS in London also singled out Hoogovens as one of Europe's most profitable steel firms with a current operating profit margin of 9.4 percent compared with 6.6 percent for VA Stahl or 4.4 percent for Usinor Sacilor.

"Generally steel companies have been more profitable in the current downturn than they would have been a few years ago, and Hoogovens is probably one of the best examples of a company which has shown a substantial improvement," he said.
The whole sector should benefit from better market conditions in 1997, but steel and other industrial shares had probably been somewhat overlooked in this year's rally, he said.
"Steel shares are not really anticipating anything, so if you're reasonably optimistic about the general economic outlook then you can make a case for the shares," he said.
Based on their potential for profit recovery, Dupont said his favourite steel shares were Arbed, Usinor and Hoogovens.
